title: Portability across compilers, operating systems and architectures
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its relevant rules.
Trace the example and justify its behaviour.
Identify important assumptions and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a reviewed and tested exercise.

understand.concept: Portable C relies on standard language and library guarantees, avoids undocumented extensions, checks implementation-defined properties and handles differences in integer widths, alignment, file modes and toolchain behaviour.
understand.whyItMatters: Software that works on one machine may fail elsewhere if it relies on assumptions about sizes, byte order, path syntax or compiler extensions.
understand.analogy: Treat standards, interfaces and release steps as explicit contracts that make assumptions visible.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the C standard, implementation documentation or project-specific requirements.

explain.narrative:
Portable C relies on standard language and library guarantees, avoids undocumented extensions, checks implementation-defined properties and handles differences in integer widths, alignment, file modes and toolchain behaviour.

State assumptions and constraints, consult the applicable standard or tool documentation, and verify the result with appropriate compiler diagnostics and tests. Separate portable guarantees from implementation-specific behaviour.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: CHAR_BIT and INT_MAX expose implementation properties. UINT32_MAX is defined when the corresponding exact-width unsigned type is available.

practise.guidedTask: List three assumptions that can make C code non-portable.
practise.independentTask: Build and test a small project with two compilers or target environments. Record differences and remove unnecessary assumptions.
hints: Use standard types and headers rather than assuming int is 32 bits.
Check feature availability and compiler extensions explicitly.
Avoid hard-coded structure layouts and platform-specific path assumptions.
